title: Elsa Schiaparelli's baroque fantasy
gist: A review of the V&A's 'Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art' (110 outfits and 50 artworks, running to 8 November 2026) that credits Elsa Schiaparelli's value to her embedding in the Parisian Surrealist network — Dalí, Giacometti, Cocteau, Man Ray, Duchamp — but faults the show for omitting her signature shocking pink and for scattering revived-house designs by Daniel Roseberry among the originals instead of ending with them, as a recent Dior exhibition did.

insights.claim: The V&A's 'Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art', running in London until 8 November 2026, assembles 110 outfits and 50 artworks plus accessories, jewellery, paintings, photographs, furniture, perfumes and archive material.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Scale and run length set the terms for a major museum attendance driver and for the associated market attention on Schiaparelli-era couture.
insights.locator: Did Elsa Schiaparelli create something more

insights.claim: The exhibition's biggest failure is the near-total absence of shocking pink, Schiaparelli's trademark and favourite colour, which she described in her 1954 memoir Shocking Life as bright, impossible and impudent — a strange omission for a show arguing she was an artist.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: The identifying brand asset was left out of the definitive institutional retelling — a curatorial choice that weakens the very case the show sets out to make.
insights.quote: Bright, impossible, impudent, becoming, life-giving, like all the lights and the birds and the fish in the world put together, a colour of China and Peru but not of the West
insights.locator: Where this rich and absorbing exhibition falters

insights.claim: The show's scenography is muted, in cool shades of grey, leaning toward contemporary minimalism that entirely misses Schiaparelli's enchanting oddness and surreal idea of beauty, and it also largely omits the cross-discipline displays the V&A usually excels at.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: A concrete critique of default museum minimalism as a mismatch for maximalist subjects — the mounting style undercuts the artist's thesis.
insights.locator: Though the lighting and soundscape are atmospheric

insights.claim: Schiaparelli's artistic credibility was built through network access: via Gabrielle Buffet-Picabia she met Man Ray and Marcel Duchamp, and she collaborated on creations with Salvador Dalí, Alberto Giacometti and Jean Cocteau.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Collaboration with named artists is what converts commercial fashion output into museum-grade cultural capital — the mechanism behind later revaluation.

insights.claim: Coco Chanel, who loathed Schiaparelli as a direct competitor, dismissed her as 'the Italian artist who makes clothes' — a backhanded compliment that inadvertently confirmed the artist framing the V&A now advances.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Competitor derision that becomes the eventual positioning — a reminder that a rival's insult can define a brand's durable differentiation.
insights.quote: the Italian artist who makes clothes
insights.locator: Coco Chanel, who loathed her as a direct competitor

insights.claim: Dalí argued the crucible of avant-garde Parisian creativity was not the café in Place Blanche where the Surrealists gathered and quarrelled but Schiaparelli's couture house itself, and Cocteau described her Place Vendôme establishment as a devil's laboratory.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Relocates the centre of a movement from its café salon to a commercial atelier — commerce as the actual site of innovation, not its downstream beneficiary.
insights.quote: Her establishment in the Place Vendôme is a devil’s laboratory. Women who go there fall into a trap, and come out masked, disguised, deformed or reformed, according to Schiaparelli’s whim.
insights.locator: Schiaparelli often visited the Palace of Versailles

insights.claim: Schiaparelli made the cover of Time magazine in 1934, mainstream validation that came while she was still in her creative ascent rather than posthumously.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Distinguishes her from artists rediscovered after death: her cultural standing was contemporaneous, so the current show is a restoration rather than a discovery.
insights.locator: In 1934 Schiaparelli made the cover of Time magazine.

insights.claim: Schiaparelli's most durable designs were deliberately transgressive artefacts — a 'Skeleton' evening dress in black crepe with quilted spine and ribs, the Dalí-painted 'Lobster' gown worn by Wallis Simpson, a 'Medusa' wedding veil undermining bridal convention, and gloves painted with a fingernail effect.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Provocation as a design system, not one-off stunts — the template later luxury houses reuse to generate press-driven brand equity.
insights.locator: The exhibition features some of her most daring designs

insights.claim: Her technical experimentation ran ahead of the market: she used fabric made of glass, produced trompe-l'oeil knitwear, and in London in 1931 wore wide-legged culottes that were widely criticised as unfeminine.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Early criticism of a garment that later became standard is the classic pattern of premature innovation being repriced decades later.
insights.locator: Schiaparelli experimented with fabric made of glass

insights.claim: Schiaparelli's appeal was two-fold and apparently contradictory: she was simultaneously a creator of phantasmagoria speaking the visual language of the wondrous and a translator of the machine age of aeroplanes and skyscrapers, with Harper's Bazaar in April 1932 crediting her clothes with the essence of modern architecture, thought and movement.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Holding two opposed aesthetics at once is the source of her staying power — a positioning lesson for any brand caught between heritage and futurism.
insights.quote: she gives her clothes the essence of modern architecture, modern thought and modern movement
insights.locator: The exhibition brings into focus Schiaparelli’s two-fold appeal

insights.claim: Schiaparelli did not sew and described her activity as 'inventing' clothes rather than making them, having begun with Modernist sportswear before Surrealism infused her work.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Creative direction detached from craft execution — the structure of the modern designer-as-brand-director role, established a century ago.
insights.locator: It was in the City of Light that Schiaparelli met

insights.claim: Schiaparelli closed her house in 1954 and the brand was revived only in 2012 as Maison Schiaparelli, now under American creative director Daniel Roseberry — a 58-year dormancy before relaunch.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: Evidence that a dormant couture name can be reactivated decades later — the underlying logic of heritage-brand acquisition and revival.

insights.claim: By scattering Roseberry's bigger and bolder creations throughout alongside the originals rather than, as a recent Dior exhibition did successfully, ending the show with contemporary designs, the V&A turned the revived house's work into a distraction from the historical arc.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: A specific, transferable curatorial rule for brand-sponsored retrospectives: segregate contemporary output at the end or it cannibalises the archive's authority.
insights.locator: Rather than trace the historical arc

insights.claim: The reviewer's verdict is that following an inventor like Schiaparelli inevitably lapses at least some of the time into pastiche or caricature, so it is the original 1930s work that feels timelessly modern.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: The archive, not the revival, holds the durable value — relevant to how heritage-brand equity is actually distributed between original and licensed output.
insights.locator: It is understandably difficult to follow in the footsteps

insights.claim: Schiaparelli's cultural persistence is evidenced in literature: in Muriel Spark's The Girls of Slender Means, set in 1945 London, a single shared Schiaparelli evening dress functions almost as a character and, during a fire, becomes the embodiment of heartless evil when a resident salvages it instead of helping others escape.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
insights.so_what: A brand embedded deeply enough in cultural memory to carry moral weight in fiction — the strongest form of intangible-asset durability.
insights.locator: The clothes designed by legendary Parisian couturière
